Read About Riyadh

Riyadh spent most of the twentieth century as a walled desert town few outsiders ever saw. It is now one of the fastest-changing cities on earth, and the change is deliberate.

The oasis that became a capital

Riyadh sits at around 600 metres above sea level on the Najd plateau — a high desert interior that is hotter than the Gulf coasts in summer and cold enough in January for frost. It is about as far from the sea as it is possible to be in the Arabian Peninsula. For most of recorded history, this geographic fact made Riyadh a place of secondary importance: settlements on the coasts had the trade routes, the pearl fisheries, the contact with the world. The Najd interior was left to its own logic, which was largely the logic of oasis agriculture, herding, and the complicated tribal politics of a landlocked region where water was rare and alliances were everything.

Riyadh itself emerged as a distinct settlement in the 1740s, when it became the seat of the ruling family of the Ad-Diriyah emirate. The city that exists today — the sprawling low-slung megacity of seven million people ringed by highways and punctuated by glass towers — bears almost no physical relationship to that earlier place. The old mud-brick town was demolished systematically from the 1950s onward as oil money arrived and the Saudi government decided that the capital of a modern nation should look like one. What replaced it was built fast, built big, and built primarily for cars.

The result is a city of jarring contrasts. Drive along King Fahad Road, the central artery, and you pass the 302-metre Kingdom Centre Tower with its inverted arch — one of the most distinctive skyscraper profiles in the world — then turn into a side street and find a neighbourhood of low buildings and corner shops that has changed little in forty years. Riyadh contains multitudes that it has not yet had the time to integrate.

Dir'iyah and the founding of Saudi Arabia

About twenty-five kilometres northwest of central Riyadh, in a limestone-walled wadi called Wadi Hanifah, stands the ruin that explains everything. Dir'iyah was the original capital of the Al Saud dynasty — the seat from which Abdulaziz ibn Muhammad ibn Saud and the religious reformer Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab launched the First Saudi State in the mid-eighteenth century. The alliance they formed, between temporal authority and a strict interpretation of Sunni Islam, became the theological and political foundation of what is now the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Three Saudi states rose and fell between the 1740s and 1902; their combined history spans the same period as the United States.

The At-Turaif district — now a UNESCO World Heritage Site — is what survives of that first capital: a plateau citadel of mud-brick palaces, mosques, and civic buildings abandoned after an Ottoman military campaign destroyed Dir'iyah in 1818. The ruins were left largely undisturbed for nearly two centuries, which is why they survive. Walk through the At-Turaif gates today and the scale of what was here is legible: this was a functioning city, not a village, with administrative buildings, royal quarters, and a water-management system sophisticated enough to support a large population on a desert plateau.

The moment that connects Dir'iyah to modern Riyadh is January 15, 1902. On that night, Abdulaziz ibn Saud — the future king, then twenty-two years old — led forty followers across the desert from Kuwait to recapture Riyadh from the Rashid family who had taken it. He stormed the Masmak Fortress, killed the Rashid governor, and by morning held the city. That act began the third and final consolidation of Saudi power, which culminated in the proclamation of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932. The Masmak Fortress still stands in the Al Dirah district, and the broken spear tip from that assault is still embedded in its original teak door.

Oil, isolation, and the speed of change

The discovery of oil in commercial quantities in the Eastern Province in 1938 set in motion a transformation that is still underway. Saudi Arabia's petroleum reserves are among the largest on earth — proven reserves that have funded everything from Riyadh's highway system to its universities to the welfare state that provides Saudi citizens with subsidised fuel, utilities, and healthcare. The speed at which a small Najdi town became a major world city is without parallel. As recently as 1950, Riyadh's population was around 50,000. Today it exceeds seven million.

For most of the twentieth century, that growth happened in near-total isolation from international tourism. Saudi Arabia did not issue tourist visas — the country admitted pilgrims to Mecca and Medina, businesspeople on specific visas, and almost no one else. Riyadh was, by policy, off-limits to casual international travellers. This began to change in 2019, when Saudi Arabia opened a tourist visa programme for the first time in its history. The change is directly connected to Vision 2030, the economic diversification plan announced in 2016 by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, which sets targets for reducing the economy's dependence on oil and developing tourism as a major revenue source.

The effects are visible everywhere in the city. Entertainment that was banned or severely restricted a decade ago — cinemas, concerts, mixed-gender social venues — now operates openly. Women drive. International restaurants, fashion brands, and entertainment companies that would not have operated here five years ago now have flagship locations in Riyadh. Boulevard Riyadh City, the vast open-air entertainment district in the north of the city, opened in 2021 and draws millions of visitors a year. The Riyadh Season festival, which runs for months each year, has brought in performers and spectacles that would have been unimaginable in Saudi Arabia a decade ago.

What Riyadh is slowly becoming

The question Riyadh is living with right now is whether the pace of change can be maintained without fracturing the social consensus that makes the Kingdom function. Saudi Arabia is not a democracy; the Al Saud family rules, the religious establishment has historically constrained social policy, and the relationship between those two forces has been renegotiated — sometimes violently — throughout the country's history. What Vision 2030 represents, among other things, is a decision by the current leadership that the religious restrictions of the past fifty years are incompatible with the economic future the country needs. The social transformation and the economic transformation are inseparable.

What the visitor sees is the surface of that negotiation: a city that is simultaneously conservative and rapidly liberalising, proud of its history and urgently remaking itself, deeply Islamic and increasingly cosmopolitan. The prayer times still interrupt the day — restaurants close their doors, shops pull down their grilles, the city pauses five times in every twenty-four hours — but the pause is shorter than it used to be, and enforced less rigidly than it once was. The abaya is no longer legally required for women in public spaces, though many women still wear it. The morality police that once patrolled the streets no longer operate with the same authority.

Dir'iyah was the capital of a Saudi state before the United States existed. Riyadh is attempting to become an international city in the span of a single generation.

What to carry into Riyadh: an awareness that you are visiting a place in the middle of a compressed, deliberate, and not entirely predictable social transformation. The monuments are real — At-Turaif and the Masmak Fortress carry genuine history — and the modernity is real too. The Kingdom Centre Tower and the KAFD skyline are not imitations of somewhere else; they are Saudi Arabia's own attempt to build the visual vocabulary of a twenty-first-century capital. Whether the whole project holds together is a question that no one can answer yet. But the ambition is serious, and Riyadh is one of the few places on earth where you can watch a country actively deciding what it wants to be.
